title: Parabolic Short
teaches: The parabolic short as we trade it: a stock that has already run far goes vertical for 3 to 5 days, gaps up on the climax day on record volume, and is shorted at market only after it cracks back under VWAP; the stop sits a few cents over the day's high, the size comes from that wide stop, the target is the daily 9 EMA within a few sessions, and a reclaim of the high, a passed window or a squeeze through the 2R gap ceiling ends it.

facts.quote: Two days of volume expansion, with each day's volume higher than the last.
facts.claim: Bracco's fourth box: two days of rising volume.

questions.q: In one line, what is a Parabolic Short?
choices: A short of a vertical run as it cracks
Shorting any stock under its 200-day
A short at the top before the crack
A long bought as a crash day turns
questions.answer: A short of a vertical run as it cracks
questions.why: A short of a vertical run as it cracks. Bracco: the burst is a 3-5 day move, the final leg of a parabolic run. It follows a big advance, large caps up 50% or more and small caps 300% or more. We short only after the crack, never the run itself. It is a mean-reversion trade that sometimes, not always, marks a lasting top.
questions.lesson_line: You short the crack of a vertical run, never the run itself.

wrong.Shorting any stock under its 200-day: This setup lives far above its 200-day, in one of the hottest stocks in the market.
wrong.A short at the top before the crack: Shorting at the day's highs can be a dangerous trap. We wait for the break back under VWAP.
wrong.A long bought as a crash day turns: That is the Parabolic Long, the mirror image: a burst down, bought on the intraday turn.

questions.simple: We short a stock that went vertical, but only once it starts to crack, never while it is still climbing.

reasons: defines the setup by the owner's house definition (B26)

questions.q: Our rule says no shorts above the 200-day, with one exception. Which short is it?
choices: A parabolic short, as Bracco has it
Any short once a stock is up 50%
A short taken while the market is Red
A short at an obvious round number
questions.answer: A parabolic short, as Bracco has it
questions.why: A parabolic short. Our rule is shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless the short is a parabolic short. Bracco's post is what defines one. A big percent gain does not open that door. A Red market does not open it either.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day there is one short we take, and Bracco's post says what it is.

wrong.Any short once a stock is up 50%: A percent gain is not the test. The exception is the parabolic short, as Bracco defines it.
wrong.A short taken while the market is Red: The market reading is not what lets a short sit above the 200-day. The parabolic definition is.
wrong.A short at an obvious round number: Round numbers are where climax points often come. They are not an exception to the 200-day rule.

questions.simple: Our 200-day rule has one exception, the parabolic short as Bracco defines it.

reasons: one cited fact only (B26, h01) carries the key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
the exception test is held (D-040); the key uses only B26's own words

questions.q: Bracco will not take the climax-day short without a gap up on the climax day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Bracco writes that you never know exactly when the climax day will hit, but he won't short without that gap-up. Our criteria card requires it too: the climax day must open above the prior close. A gap of 5% or more is stronger. Any open above the prior close meets the rule.
questions.lesson_line: No gap up, no climax-day short.
questions.simple: True, because Bracco says he will not short a climax day unless it gaps up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook and the criteria card (the climax gap is settled there; the owner may loosen it)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The target of a Parabolic Short is the daily ___ EMA.
questions.why: 9. The 9 EMA is the exponential moving average of the daily closes, so recent days count most. Bracco calls it a magnet for mean reversion: a stretched stock tends to get pulled back toward it. That makes it the level you cover at, so know where it sits before you short. Our rule names the 9-day average as this setup's target.
questions.lesson_line: The trade runs to the 9 EMA. Know where it sits before you short.
questions.simple: The target is the daily 9 EMA, which Bracco says pulls a stretched stock back like a magnet.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D47) plus Bracco's post
how much comes off at the 9 EMA is held (D-013); the key is the level only

questions.q: Where does the stop sit on a Parabolic Short?
choices: A few cents over the day's high
A few cents under the low
At the 9 EMA, below the price
A fixed 3% above your fill
questions.answer: A few cents over the day's high
questions.why: A few cents over the climax day's high. Bracco's thesis is that the top is in, so the day's high is the line. Our card puts the stop a few cents over the high at the time of entry. Kullamagi agrees: the stop is the highs of the day. It is a level on the chart, not a percent of your fill.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is over the day's high. If that goes, the top was not in.

wrong.A few cents under the low: That is a long's stop. A short's stop sits above price.
wrong.At the 9 EMA, below the price: The 9 EMA is the target, not the stop. A short's stop sits above price.
wrong.A fixed 3% above your fill: The stop is a level on the chart, the day's high, not a percent.

questions.simple: The stop goes a few cents over the day's high, because if price gets back there the top was not in.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D47) and the criteria card (settled stop)

questions.q: On the climax day you short the gap up at the open, before the high is set.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. After the gap up, nothing at the open. The short comes later, when the stock breaks back under VWAP after the high is set, usually 10 to 60 minutes in. Shorting at the day's highs can be a dangerous trap. Kullamagi: do not be early, and let the amateur shorts get run over.
questions.lesson_line: The open is for watching. The crack is for shorting.
questions.simple: False. After the gap up we do nothing at the open, because shorting at the day's highs is a dangerous trap.

reasons: rests on the card's proposed open-wait rule

questions.q: Which of these is one of Bracco's burst boxes?
choices: Two straight overnight gap ups
A close under the 50-day
Volume falling for two days
A ten-week base before it
questions.answer: Two straight overnight gap ups
questions.why: Two straight overnight gap ups. Bracco's boxes are three straight up days and two straight overnight gap ups. Add two of three days of range expansion and two days of rising volume. Then a gap up on the climax day. Not every box must be checked, but the more that are, the stronger the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Count the boxes: up days, gap ups, bigger gains, rising volume, the climax gap.

wrong.A close under the 50-day: A burst runs far above its averages. A close under the 50-day is a different chart.
wrong.Volume falling for two days: The box is rising volume, each day higher than the last.
wrong.A ten-week base before it: The boxes count the burst's last days, not the base before it.

questions.simple: Two straight overnight gap ups is one of Bracco's boxes for a burst.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26's box list)
the count of boxes needed is held (D-040); only the boxes themselves are keyed

questions.q: The climax day gaps up, runs higher for 20 minutes, then turns. What is the first entry?
choices: The break back under VWAP
The first print at the open
The first green 5-minute bar
A daily close under the 9 EMA
questions.answer: The break back under VWAP
questions.why: The break back under VWAP. Bracco: typically 10 to 60 minutes after the open, sellers emerge and the stock starts to reverse. He calls that pattern the U-Turn. The first entry is a breakdown below VWAP, and he never enters before that. Our card says short on that break after the high is set. It is not the open, a green bar or a daily close.
questions.lesson_line: The first entry is the VWAP break after the high is set.

wrong.The first green 5-minute bar: A green bar is strength. The entry is the break down, under VWAP.
wrong.A daily close under the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA is where the trade ends, not where it starts.
wrong.The first print at the open: Nothing at the open. The high is not set yet.

questions.simple: You short the first time price breaks back under VWAP after the high is set, not at the open.

reasons: the card's VWAP trigger is a proposed rule (ps.vwap_trigger)
several agreeing quotes

questions.q: On daily bars, the stand-in for the intraday crack is a climax day that closes above its open.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. On daily bars the stand-in for the intraday crack is a climax day that closes under its open. It opens higher and closes lower. Shorting a green climax day won 23% of the time. The real trigger is the break under VWAP, which a daily bar cannot show.
questions.lesson_line: Opens higher, closes lower: that is the crack on a daily chart.
questions.simple: False. On a daily chart the crack is a close under the open, and shorting a green climax day won only 23% of the time.

reasons: the 23% is a result from our own scan
rests on the card's daily-bar stand-in

questions.q: Tap the days that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: Bracco's parabolic burst, the final leg of a run, usually lasts ___ days.
questions.answer: 3 to 5
questions.why: 3 to 5. Bracco: the parabolic burst is a 3-5 day move that marks the final leg. In his studies most bursts last 3 to 5 days. Kullamagi also wants the stock up 3 to 5 or more days in a row. Most is not all. The run before the burst can be longer, as in GDS, a 13-session run.
questions.lesson_line: A burst is short, about 3 to 5 days, and the climax gap comes late in it.
questions.simple: A burst lasts about 3 to 5 days, and it is only the last leg of a longer run.

reasons: a stable definition with agreeing quotes from two publishers

questions.q: By Kullamagi's rule, how far has a larger-cap stock run before it is a candidate?
choices: 50% to 100% or more in days or weeks
10% to 20% in the past few months
300% to 1,000% or more in days or weeks
The run does not matter; the gap does
questions.answer: 50% to 100% or more in days or weeks
questions.why: 50% to 100% or more in days or weeks. Kullamagi's floor for a larger cap is a stock up 50-100%+ in a few days or weeks. A smaller cap needs 300-1000%+. Our card takes 50% or more for large caps. The run is only the entry ticket. Bracco calls judging by percent gain alone a frequent mistake, so the chart's shape must fit too.
questions.lesson_line: A big run comes first. Half again its price, at least, in days or weeks.

wrong.The run does not matter; the gap does: The gap ends a run. Without the large advance there is nothing to exhaust.
wrong.10% to 20% in the past few months: That is far below Kullamagi's floor of 50%. It is an ordinary move, not a parabolic run.
wrong.300% to 1,000% or more in days or weeks: That is his bar for a smaller cap, not a larger one.

questions.simple: A larger-cap stock must be up 50% to 100% or more in days or weeks first, by Kullamagi's rule.

reasons: the cap bands are one author's rule (Kullamagi) plus the card's proposed floor
small-cap bands are held (D-122); only the larger-cap floor is keyed

questions.q: Is this our Parabolic Short?
choices: No; the run is still too young
Yes; the gap and red close fit it
Yes; the gap up is the trigger
No; the gap is under the 5% minimum
questions.answer: No; the run is still too young
questions.why: No. A stock in week one out of a long base is not this setup. Bracco calls that kind of trade very short lived. RGTI fit this case: fresh out of a base, it made a new high on day 6 and took the stop. Size does not fix a wrong setup.
questions.lesson_line: Right candle, wrong week. A stock just out of a base is not this setup.

wrong.Yes; the gap and red close fit it: The daily shape fits, the context does not. Three days out of a base is not an exhausted run.
wrong.No; the gap is under the 5% minimum: 5% or more is the stronger mark, not a minimum. Any gap up passes the gate. The young run is the problem.
wrong.Yes; the gap up is the trigger: The gap is the setup, and the trigger is the break under VWAP. A stock this young has no setup.

questions.story: A stock broke out of a six-month base three days ago. Two up days, then today it gaps up 4% and closes red.
questions.simple: No. A stock only three days out of a six-month base is too young a run to be exhausted.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26) and the card's not-this-setup list

questions.q: A hard-to-borrow stock with a high borrow fee is skipped, even on a perfect climax day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our rule is to skip a short when the stock is hard to borrow or the borrow fee is high. The card asks for shares available to borrow at a fair fee, and squeeze names are often hard to borrow. Kullamagi has locates through his brokers that most retail brokers do not offer.
questions.lesson_line: No borrow, no trade. The chart does not pay the fee.
questions.simple: True, because we skip any short we cannot borrow at a fair fee.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D48)

questions.q: The VWAP break prints. What order do you send?
choices: A market order, sent at once
A limit order a few cents lower
A sell-stop under the day's low
Wait for the 5-minute bar to close
questions.answer: A market order, sent at once
questions.why: A market order, sent at once. Our entries are market orders. The trigger has printed and the stop is already known, so there is nothing to wait for. A limit order is not how we enter. Bracco's second entry, at the break of the day's low, is not taught: one entry, full size, one stop.
questions.lesson_line: When the trigger prints, you are in at market.

wrong.A sell-stop under the day's low: That is Bracco's second entry, which we do not take. One entry, at the VWAP break.
wrong.A limit order a few cents lower: Our entries are market orders, not limit orders.
wrong.Wait for the 5-minute bar to close: The trigger is the break under VWAP, not a bar close.

questions.simple: Send a market order right when the VWAP break prints, because our entries are market orders.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, one entry, settled)

questions.q: What now?
choices: Out; the high is reclaimed
Hold; it is only a few cents
Widen the stop to 54.00
Add; the thesis still holds
questions.answer: Out; the high is reclaimed
questions.why: Out. The stop sat at 52.56, a few cents over the high, and the stock now trades 52.60. If the price reclaims the day's high, the thesis or the timing was wrong, and you exit. The stop is the exit and it never widens. Parabolic advances often go further than anyone thinks, so you do not add either.
questions.lesson_line: The day's high is the line. Over it, you are wrong, and wrong is flat.

wrong.Hold; it is only a few cents: A few cents over the high is over the high. A new high means the top was not in.
wrong.Widen the stop to 54.00: The stop never widens. Parabolic advances go further than anyone thinks.
wrong.Add; the thesis still holds: Bracco never adds when he is down. Neither do we.

questions.story: You shorted the VWAP break at 48.50. Your stop line, over the day's high, is 52.56. At 2 pm it trades 52.60.
questions.simple: Get out, because price is back over the day's high, so the top was not in.

deeper.example: A reclaim can come after a long wait. PLUG's climax was 2021-01-13. A marginal higher high eight sessions later took the stop, and the real top came on 2021-01-26. Out is still out, even when the stock then turns.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop never widens; settled)

questions.q: On the climax day, what should the volume look like?
choices: The highest of the whole run
Lighter than the day before
Average; volume does not matter
Heavy only in the last hour
questions.answer: The highest of the whole run
questions.why: The highest of the whole run. Bracco: the climax day almost invariably shows the highest opening volume of the entire run. A big spike after a massive move signals exhaustion. StockCharts says an exhaustion gap also shows high volume. Our card wants the day's volume, and ideally its first 5 to 15 minutes, the highest of the run. It is a tell, not a trigger. The trigger is the break under VWAP.
questions.lesson_line: The crowd buys the top. Record volume on the climax day is the tell.

wrong.Lighter than the day before: Lighter volume is not a climax. The card wants a record; rising but not a record is only a B- mark.
wrong.Average; volume does not matter: Volume is half of Bracco's first two checks: range and volume expansion.
wrong.Heavy only in the last hour: The record volume comes at the open, in the first minutes of the gap.

questions.simple: Volume should be the highest of the whole run, since a huge spike after a big move signals exhaustion.

reasons: wrong note fixed before (B- row wording)

questions.q: A stock that climbed in steady stair-steps for a year is a Parabolic Short once it is up 100%.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Bracco says to avoid a steady, controlled ascent for Parabolic Shorts: it reflects sustained strength and can persist for an extended period. He also names judging by percent gain alone, without the chart's structure, as a frequent mistake. Our card agrees: a steady, linear trend however far it has run is not this setup, as with AAPL in 2023.
questions.lesson_line: Percent gain is not the test. Shape is. Stair-steps are not a parabola.
questions.simple: False, because a steady climb shows lasting strength, and the size of the gain alone does not make a stock parabolic.

reasons: the card's not-this line (c09) is a proposed rule; Bracco's own words agree

questions.q: Short the VWAP break today?
choices: No; a report inside 3 sessions
No; a 9% gap is too big to short
Yes; the setup triggered today
Yes; at half the usual size
questions.answer: No; a report inside 3 sessions
questions.why: No. We take no new short within 3 sessions of a report, and this one reports after tomorrow's close. The account rule is no new trades in the 3 days before an earnings report. Hold through one only if the trade is up 5R. A textbook burst and a big gap do not change that.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings inside three days is a pass, however good the chart.

wrong.Yes; the setup triggered today: The trigger fired and the calendar still says no. The earnings rule is a hard line.
wrong.Yes; at half the usual size: Size does not fix report risk. Smaller is still in.
wrong.No; a 9% gap is too big to short: The gap is part of the setup, not the problem. A gap of 5% or more is stronger. The report is why we pass.

questions.story: The burst is textbook and the climax day gaps up 9%. Earnings come after the close tomorrow.
questions.simple: No, because a report is due inside 3 sessions, and we take no new short that close to earnings.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, settled)

questions.q: The prior close is 42.00 and the climax day opens at 48.47. How big is the gap up?
questions.why: 15.4%. The gap is the open minus the prior close: 48.47 minus 42.00. Divide by the prior close, 42.00, and show it as a percent. Our card needs the climax day to open above the prior close, and a gap of 5% or more is stronger. GDS also gapped 15.4%, on record volume, and closed red. The prices here are made up for the drill.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap in percent. A gap of 5% or more is the stronger one.
questions.simple: The open is 15.4 percent above the prior close, which is a big gap up.

reasons: a computed key (percent change)

wrong.13.3%: Divided by the open. The gap is measured against the prior close.
wrong.115.4%: Divided the open by the prior close and forgot to subtract 1.
wrong.6.5%: Read the dollar gap as a percent. Divide it by the prior close first.

questions.q: The climax day is Tuesday. You are stopped out of the short that day. Wednesday it cracks under VWAP again. Allowed?
choices: Yes; a new trigger in the window
No; one try per climax move
Yes; keep Tuesday's stop
No; a stop-out ends it
questions.answer: Yes; a new trigger in the window
questions.why: Yes. After a stop-out we short again only if the setup triggers again. It is a new trade with its own stop and every rule. The idea has a 1 to 2 day window, and Wednesday is the day after the climax, inside it. One stock gets at most 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a verdict. The next trigger is a new trade, inside the window.

wrong.No; one try per climax move: The cap is 3 tries in a week and 6 in a month, not one.
wrong.Yes; keep Tuesday's stop: A new trade has its own stop, set at its own entry.
wrong.No; a stop-out ends it: One stop-out does not close it. Two failed triggers, or the window passing, drops the idea.

questions.simple: Yes, because after a stop-out a new trigger inside the 1 to 2 day window is a new trade with its own stop.

deeper.trap: A second failed trigger ends it. Our card drops the idea when the trigger fails twice or the window passes. That holds even if the cap of 3 tries a week is not used up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B21 and E56, settled)

questions.q: We short parabolic names only at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our rule is to trade only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. The card asks for a price of $10 or more and $20 million or more traded a day on average. It is a floor to pass before any chart is read, not a sign to short.
questions.lesson_line: Liquidity first. A price of $10 and $20 million a day are the floor.
questions.simple: True, because we trade only stocks priced at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B23, settled)

questions.q: Tap the name that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Bracco's favorite climax-day pattern, a run at the open then a break under VWAP, is the ___.
questions.answer: U-Turn
questions.why: The U-Turn. Bracco's preferred intraday pattern, the most prevalent on the climax day. The gap runs higher, then 10 to 60 minutes in sellers emerge and it breaks under VWAP. On our card a clean U-Turn is the A+ row for the trigger. That means a run at the open, then a fast break under VWAP and the day's low.
questions.lesson_line: A run at the open, then a fast break under VWAP: the U-Turn.
questions.simple: It is the U-Turn, Bracco's favorite pattern, where a run at the open turns into a break under VWAP.

reasons: Bracco's own naming; the A+ row is the card's

questions.q: By Bracco, when is a Parabolic Short complete?
choices: At the 9 EMA test on the backside
When it falls 50% from the high
When it closes under the 200-day
The next morning, whatever happens
questions.answer: At the 9 EMA test on the backside
questions.why: At the 9 EMA test on the backside of the move. Bracco: once the 9 EMA is tested on the backside, he considers the Parabolic Short complete. That is his target and our rule's target. This setup is paid at the 9 EMA, inside a few sessions, or not at all.
questions.lesson_line: The trade is done at the 9 EMA. Do not wait for a crash.

wrong.When it falls 50% from the high: No cited fact makes a fixed fall the target. The 9 EMA is.
wrong.When it closes under the 200-day: The stock sits far above its 200-day. The target is much nearer: the 9 EMA.
wrong.The next morning, whatever happens: Time is not the target. The 9 EMA is, and it is paid inside a few sessions or not at all.

questions.simple: Bracco counts the trade as done once the stock tests the 9 EMA on the way back down.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D47)
how much comes off at the 9 EMA is held (D-013); only the level is keyed

questions.q: The prior close is 48.50 and the 9-day EMA sits at 40.00. How far above the average is that close?
questions.why: 21.25%. The stretch is the close minus the average: 48.50 minus 40.00. Divide by the average, 40.00, and show it as a percent. We read a chart in percents: how far a stock is stretched above its averages. Bracco's checklist lists percent extensions from moving averages and ATR multiples from the 50-day. This only measures the stretch. It is not a cut-off.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the stretch in percent before you call anything parabolic.
questions.simple: The close is 21.25 percent above the 9-day average: the difference divided by the average.

reasons: a computed key (percent change)
the extension floor is held (D-040); this question computes a percent only

wrong.121.25%: Divided the close by the average and forgot to subtract 1.
wrong.82.47%: Gave the average as a share of the close.
wrong.212.50%: Slipped the decimal point one place right.

questions.q: Shorted at 29.66 with the stop at 31.81. How wide is the stop, as a percent of the fill?
questions.why: 7.25%. The stop width is the stop minus the fill: 31.81 minus 29.66. Divide by the fill, 29.66, and show it as a percent. We prefer a stop 1-3% away, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% is acceptable. This one is past 5%, so we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. These are BILI's numbers, listed at 7.2% in our data.
questions.lesson_line: A stop past 5% is too wide to take. Wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.simple: The stop is 7.25 percent from the fill. That is past what we accept, so we wait for a tighter trigger.

deeper.example: On our daily-bar read of BILI, a stop 7.2% away still saw the 9 EMA in 4 sessions and 3R on day 4. It worked, but that stop is past the 5% we accept, so we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.

reasons: a computed key (stop width in percent)
stop width options are held (D-005); only A13's 3% and A5's size-from-the-stop are keyed

wrong.2.15%: Read the dollar gap as a percent. Divide it by the fill first.

questions.q: Account 50,000. Risk 0.5%. Short 48.50, stop 52.56. How many shares does the risk allow?
questions.answer: 61 shares
questions.why: 61 shares. The risk dollars are 50,000 x 0.5%. The stop distance is 52.56 minus 48.50. Divide the risk dollars by the stop distance and round down to 61. Rounding down keeps the risk at or under 0.5%. The position cap can only make the size smaller. Stop first, size last. If the honest stop does not fit, skip.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last. The same on the short side.
questions.simple: Risk 0.5 percent of the account, divide by the stop distance, and round down to 61 shares.

reasons: a computed key (position size from risk)

choices: 62 shares
123 shares
61 shares
5 shares

wrong.62 shares: Rounded up. That pushes the risk over 0.5%, so always round down.
wrong.123 shares: Doubled the risk percent. Use the 0.5% the question gives.
wrong.5 shares: Divided the risk dollars by the fill price, not by the stop distance.

questions.q: Short it now?
choices: No; wait for the break under VWAP
Yes; the gap is the trigger
Yes; a small starter short here
No; never short into a gap-up day
questions.answer: No; wait for the break under VWAP
questions.why: No. After the gap up, nothing at the open. The gap is the setup. The trigger is the break back under VWAP after the high is set, usually 10 to 60 minutes in. Shorting at the day's highs is a dangerous trap. Stamatoudis would rather miss the move than be chopped up by many rapid early attempts. Everyone calling the top is not a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: The crowd screaming top is not a trigger. The VWAP break is.

wrong.Yes; the gap is the trigger: The gap is the setup. The trigger is the break under VWAP after the high is set.
wrong.Yes; a small starter short here: Small and early is still early. Let the amateur shorts get run over first.
wrong.No; never short into a gap-up day: A gap up that cracks is exactly this trade. The timing is the point, not the gap.

questions.story: The climax day gaps up 9% and runs higher in the first 10 minutes. Everyone is calling the top.
questions.simple: Wait. The gap is only the setup, and the trigger is the break back under VWAP after the high is set.

reasons: rests on the card's proposed open-wait rule

questions.q: Where is the stop now?
choices: 53.40, the first 30-minute high
52.70, the first 30-minute low
Keep 52.56; it was the rule
Get out; the gap is past 2R
questions.answer: 53.40, the first 30-minute high
questions.why: 53.40. A gap through the stop hands the decision to the first 30-minute bar. For a short, its high is the new stop. The gap rule has a ceiling of 2R: past it, get out. 53.40 is inside that ceiling, so the new stop stands. The gap rule is the one exception to a stop that never moves wider.
questions.lesson_line: A gap over the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.Keep 52.56; it was the rule: Price is already through it. The gap rule replaces it with the 30-minute high.
wrong.Get out; the gap is past 2R: 53.40 is inside the 2R ceiling. The ceiling has not been hit.
wrong.52.70, the first 30-minute low: The low is the long-side version. A short's stop sits above price, so it is the bar's high.

questions.story: Short at 48.50, stop 52.56. Next morning it gaps open at 53.00, through your stop. The first 30-minute bar runs from 52.70 to 53.40.
questions.simple: A gap through the stop gives the first 30 minutes the decision. For a short, the high of that bar, 53.40, is the new stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's gap rule (B20)

questions.q: Our rule adds a second short when the stock breaks the day's low.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Bracco's first entry is the break under VWAP, followed by a second short when the stock breaches the day's lows. Our rule is the full size at one price with one stop, no adding. The second entry is not taught.
questions.lesson_line: One entry, one stop, full size. That is the whole position.
questions.simple: False. Bracco takes a second entry, but we take one entry at full size with one stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's one-entry rule (A5)

questions.q: By our card, short it here?
choices: No; more than 4% under the break
Yes; the crack is real and clean
Yes; the stop is still over the high
No; shorts belong at the day's high
questions.answer: No; more than 4% under the break
questions.why: No. 47.50 sits more than 4% under the 50.00 break, so we skip. No chasing: never go more than 4% past the trigger, mirrored for a short. The stop stays over the high, so a late fill means a wider stop and fewer shares. A clean crack does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss it than chase it. Four percent and done, both ways.

wrong.Yes; the crack is real and clean: Real and clean can both be true and the entry still too far away. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.No; shorts belong at the day's high: Shorting at the day's highs is a dangerous trap. The entry is the break under VWAP, and this one has gone.
wrong.Yes; the stop is still over the high: The stop stays over the high, so a late fill means a wider stop and fewer shares. The chase line is 4%.

questions.story: The VWAP break printed at 50.00 while you were away. Now it trades 47.50, still well above the 9 EMA.
questions.simple: Skip it. The stock is already more than 4% under the 50.00 break, and chasing a late short is not our rule.

deeper.trap: A clean crack is not a free pass. The 4% line is about price, not about how good the chart looks. A late fill keeps the same stop over the high, so the stop is wider and the share count smaller. Miss it and wait for the next idea.

reasons: rests on the owner's no-chase rule (C28) mirrored for a short
the key needs a percent worked out from two prices

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: In a parabolic run the pauses get ___ as the price goes higher.
questions.answer: shorter
questions.why: Shorter. Bracco: ideally the consolidation periods shorten as the price surges higher, with minimal pullbacks. Our card adds the ATR rising, and a measurable form: the last 2 to 3 weekly ranges each larger than the one before. A steady linear climb does not do this, and Bracco says to avoid it.
questions.lesson_line: Parabolic means the pauses get shorter. Linear means they do not.
questions.simple: In a parabolic run the pauses get shorter and the pullbacks smaller as price climbs.

deeper.counter: A stock can be up a lot and still be linear. Percent gain alone does not make a run parabolic. Bracco calls judging by percent gain alone a frequent mistake.

reasons: stable definition with two sources

questions.q: Short the close?
choices: No; a green day, no crack
Yes; the burst must be done
Yes; tomorrow will gap down
questions.answer: No; a green day, no crack
questions.why: No. On daily bars the crack is a close under the open; shorting a green climax day won 23% of the time. Here the real top came the next day and a short at that close was stopped at 0R.
questions.lesson_line: A green climax day has not cracked. Strength is not a trigger.

wrong.Yes; the burst must be done: Nobody knows the burst is done until it cracks. Green at the close means it has not.
wrong.Yes; tomorrow will gap down: Maybe. A guess about tomorrow is not a trigger today.

questions.story: After a five-day burst the stock gaps up and never looks back. It closes 15.8% above its open, near the top of its range.

questions.q: Two climax days. One: four boxes, a 15% gap, record volume. The other: two boxes, a 2% gap, average volume. Which is stronger?
choices: The four-box day; more boxes win
The two-box day; quieter is safer
Equal; only the crack itself counts
Neither; only percent gain counts
questions.answer: The four-box day; more boxes win
questions.why: The four-box day. The more boxes checked, the stronger the setup. A gap of 5% or more is stronger, and the climax day's volume should be the highest of the run. The crack is the trigger, not the strength of the setup. Percent gain alone is no test: Bracco calls that a frequent mistake.
questions.lesson_line: More boxes, a bigger gap, a record crowd: the stronger climax.

wrong.The two-box day; quieter is safer: Quiet is not safe here. The stronger setup checks more boxes, gaps 5% or more and prints the highest volume of the run.
wrong.Equal; only the crack itself counts: The crack is the trigger. Boxes, gap and volume decide how strong the setup is.
wrong.Neither; only percent gain counts: Bracco calls relying on percent gain alone a frequent mistake. Boxes, gap and volume tell you more.

questions.simple: The four-box day is stronger. More boxes checked means a stronger setup, and a big gap on record volume points the same way.

reasons: box count and grade rows are the card's proposal (D-040 pending)
grading is discretionary (E50)

questions.q: Which of Bracco's intraday patterns is that?
choices: Long-Drawn-Out Range Breakdown
The U-Turn, a run then a VWAP break
Quick Opening Range Breakdown
The second short at the day's low
questions.answer: Long-Drawn-Out Range Breakdown
questions.why: The Long-Drawn-Out Range Breakdown: a tight range for the first one to two hours. Bracco sees it more often in setups that do not fully meet all criteria. His preferred pattern is the U-Turn, a break under VWAP 10 to 60 minutes in.
questions.lesson_line: A clean U-Turn turns 10 to 60 minutes in. Two hours of chop first is the drawn-out version.

wrong.The U-Turn, a run then a VWAP break: The U-Turn turns 10 to 60 minutes in. Two hours of range is the drawn-out version.
wrong.Quick Opening Range Breakdown: That one sets its high on the first 5-minute candle and often shows on day 1 or 2 of the burst. This day chopped for two hours first.
wrong.The second short at the day's low: That is the second short, taken after the VWAP break when the stock breaches the day's lows. Here the VWAP break is the first move.

questions.story: The climax day gaps up, then chops in a tight range for two hours before breaking under VWAP.
questions.simple: Two hours of tight range before the VWAP break is Bracco's Long-Drawn-Out Range Breakdown.

reasons: the star grades are Bracco's, not ours

questions.q: If you still hold the short, the stop moves to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. On this setup the 9 EMA usually comes first.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Our rulebook moves the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The card names 2R for this setup if the short is held. The 9 EMA cover usually comes first, so breakeven often never comes into play. The stop only moves in your favor, never wider.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven at 2R to 5R if you are still in. Usually the 9 EMA ends the trade first.
questions.simple: True. Breakeven comes at 2R to 5R if you are still in, and on this setup the 9 EMA usually ends the trade first.

reasons: rests on the owner's breakeven rule (B19), which gives a range
the card names 2R

questions.q: By our card, what now?
choices: Cover; this setup's time is up
Hold; the stop is a long way off
Add more; it has not squeezed yet
Hold until the 10-day time stop
questions.answer: Cover; this setup's time is up
questions.why: Cover. If the 9 EMA is not reached within 3 sessions of entry, cover. The 10-day time stop is only the outer limit for any trade. A far stop means fewer shares, not more patience, and we never add. TSLA touched the 9 EMA only on day 8, by then above the entry, then chopped for 25 sessions before the stop.
questions.lesson_line: This trade pays fast or not at all. Three sessions without the 9 EMA is the exit.

wrong.Hold; the stop is a long way off: A far stop is a reason for fewer shares, not for waiting. The time limit has run out.
wrong.Hold until the 10-day time stop: The 10-day rule is the outer limit for any trade. This setup's own limit is 3 sessions.
wrong.Add more; it has not squeezed yet: Never add to a parabolic short. Not squeezed yet is not a reason.

questions.story: You shorted at 99.80, stop 119.80. Three sessions later the 9 EMA is still not reached and the stock chops under its high.
questions.simple: Cover now. This setup must reach the 9 EMA within 3 sessions, and the 10-day limit is only the outer edge.

deeper.example: TSLA 2020-07-13: short 99.80, stop 119.80. It gave 0.44R at best. The 9 EMA was only touched on day 8, and by then it sat above the entry. Twenty-five sessions of chop under the climax high followed, with a report inside the window.

reasons: the 3-session limit is the card's proposal from measured medians, not an owner ruling
rests on the owner's time stop (C33)

questions.q: You shorted a climax day with the target only 0.14R away. Which yardstick fits this trade?
choices: The 9 EMA, which acts as a magnet
A fixed 3R, set before the trade
The 50-day as the target
The swing low as the target
questions.answer: The 9 EMA, which acts as a magnet
questions.why: The 9 EMA. Our rule names the 9-day average as a parabolic short's target, and Bracco calls the trade complete once it is tested. A fixed multiple of R is not the exit here, because the level sets the exit. On MSTR the 9 EMA was 0.14R away and the stock never gave more than 0.77R before chopping. That is a trade the 9 EMA target handles and a fixed 3R test cannot.
questions.lesson_line: The target is a level, not a multiple. When the level is close, the trade is small.

wrong.The 50-day as the target: Bracco's target is the 9 EMA, not the 50-day.
wrong.The swing low as the target: The rule names a moving average, not a low on the chart. Bracco's target is the 9 EMA, which acts as a magnet for mean reversion.
wrong.A fixed 3R, set before the trade: The stock never gave more than 0.77R, so a fixed 3R was never on the table here. The 9 EMA is the level this setup is judged by.

questions.simple: The target is the 9 EMA, a level and not a multiple. Here it is only 0.14R away.

reasons: rests on the owner's rule that the target is the 9-day average (D47)
MSTR figures come from our own scan

questions.q: What is the lesson?
choices: A mania can top more than once
Do not short a mania
Use a wider stop in a mania
Hold past the 9 EMA for 3R
questions.answer: A mania can top more than once
questions.why: A mania can top more than once. The cover rule takes the trade out at the 9 EMA on day 2, at 0.52R. Holding on meant the new high on day 3 took the stop. Twenty sessions later the stock was 27.7% higher. In our data, three of the four losing examples made a new high within three to ten sessions. That is what the 1 to 2 day window and the three-tries cap are for.
questions.lesson_line: A mania can top twice. Take the 9 EMA, respect the stop, and do not chase the next one.

wrong.Do not short a mania: Hot runaway stocks are exactly where this setup lives. The lesson is the window and the tries cap, not skipping it.
wrong.Use a wider stop in a mania: The stop is the exit. It never moves wider, and a few cents over the climax high is the rule.
wrong.Hold past the 9 EMA for 3R: This setup is paid at the 9 EMA, inside a few sessions, or not at all. Holding past it is how 0.52R became a stop-out.

questions.story: Shorted 60.68, stop 65.34. Day 2 touches the 9 EMA at 0.52R. Day 3 prints a new high and takes the stop. Twenty sessions later the stock is 27.7% higher.
questions.simple: A mania can top twice, so we take the 9 EMA when it comes and do not chase the next climax.

deeper.trap: Hindsight says it was a bad short. It was not: the plan paid at the 9 EMA on day 2, and the stop did its job on day 3. The lesson is the window and the tries cap, not never short a mania.

reasons: figures come from our own scan
window and tries cap rest on the owner's rulebook (E56)

questions.q: Once short, if the stock reclaims the climax day's high you may give it room by moving the stop higher.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. The stop is the exit; it never widens. Bracco: if the price reclaims the day's high, the thesis or the timing was wrong, and he exits.
questions.lesson_line: Room is how a planned loss becomes a disaster. Over the high, you are out.

questions.q: SLV, AGQ and SIVR all hit the climax scan on the same day. What does our card say about commodity ETFs?
choices: A cue against; all three lost
Strong sign; three hits confirm it
Short the most liquid one only
No difference; same rules as stocks
questions.answer: A cue against; all three lost
questions.why: A cue against. SLV, AGQ and SIVR all hit the scan on 2026-01-26. All lost on the next leg up, so three hits at once confirmed nothing. Bracco's own AGQ shorts failed 3 times over 2 sessions, and he notes parabolic advances often go further than anyone thinks. It is a cue, not a ban.
questions.lesson_line: A commodity in a frenzy does not care about your climax day.

wrong.Short the most liquid one only: Liquidity was not the problem. The next leg up was.
wrong.No difference; same rules as stocks: Our card marks commodity ETFs as a cue against, because three of them hit the scan together and all lost.
wrong.Strong sign; three hits confirm it: All three hit the scan together and all three lost, so a crowd of hits is no confirmation.

questions.simple: Treat it as a warning. SLV, AGQ and SIVR all hit the scan the same day and all lost on the next leg up.

reasons: rests on one card note from our own scan (c36)
a dated event

questions.q: By our card, what now?
choices: Out; the VWAP reclaim ends it
Hold until 33.40 is retaken
Add; VWAP is just noise
Cover half; hold the rest
questions.answer: Out; the VWAP reclaim ends it
questions.why: Out. A VWAP reclaim after a VWAP-fail entry is the exit, in full, not a trim. Kullamagi: the stop is the highs of the day, or if VWAP fails, a reclaim of the VWAP. The day's high, 33.40, is the stop for a break-under-VWAP entry. This entry was the failed bounce, so its exit is the reclaim.
questions.lesson_line: You entered on the failed bounce at VWAP. A reclaim of VWAP says the bounce did not fail.

wrong.Hold until 33.40 is retaken: The day's high is the stop for a VWAP-break entry. For a VWAP-fail entry the reclaim is the exit.
wrong.Add; VWAP is just noise: VWAP is the one intraday line Kullamagi uses. A reclaim is the thesis failing, not noise.
wrong.Cover half; hold the rest: The reclaim is a full exit, not a trim. Holding half keeps a thesis that has already failed.

questions.story: You shorted a failed bounce into VWAP at 31.20; the day's high is 33.40. An hour later it trades back above VWAP.
questions.simple: Get out. You entered on a failed bounce at VWAP, so a move back above VWAP means the bounce did not fail.

reasons: the VWAP-reclaim exit is the card's proposal
the failed-bounce entry is Kullamagi's

questions.q: What is it?
choices: A News Failure on the gap up
A Parabolic Short on the gap up
A Wedge Drop on the gap up
A Parabolic Long on the gap up
questions.answer: A News Failure on the gap up
questions.why: A News Failure shape. A good-news gap up that closes red with no burst before it. A Parabolic Short needs the 3-5 day burst first. AAOI had 2 of 4 boxes, no three straight up closes and no acceleration. It ran 2.16R, then stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Same candle, different setup. Look at the days before the gap.

wrong.A Parabolic Short on the gap up: No burst, no parabola. The slow drift before the gap is the tell.
wrong.A Wedge Drop on the gap up: A Wedge Drop comes days after a top, at the averages, under the 200-day. This is a gap up out of a slow drift.
wrong.A Parabolic Long on the gap up: A Parabolic Long needs a burst down and a gap down. This gapped up.

questions.story: A stock drifted up slowly for weeks. Today it gaps up 27.7% on a surprise headline and closes red. It had no three straight up closes and no acceleration before it.
questions.simple: It drifted up slowly, then gapped up on a headline and closed red, so it is a News Failure.

deeper.trap: The candle looks the same: a big gap up that closes red. The difference is the days before it. A Parabolic Short needs the burst first. A one-day 27.7% gap after a slow rise is the News Failure shape, which needs no burst.

reasons: figures come from our own scan

questions.q: Our card checks the last three weekly ranges. What is its read?
choices: Not parabolic; ranges did not expand
Parabolic; the red close is the crack
Parabolic; three weeks of range
Not parabolic; it is above its 200-day
questions.answer: Not parabolic; ranges did not expand
questions.why: Not parabolic. Our card wants the last 2 to 3 weekly ranges each larger than the one before. Here all three are given: 12.33, 5.27 and 13.33, so the middle week shrank. Bracco calls consecutive weeks of range expansion extremely important. This was a steady leader's one-day reversal, the linear case. NVDA gave 1.19R, then stopped. The 200-day is not the test, because our rule lets a parabolic short sit above it.
questions.lesson_line: A leader's one bad day is not a climax. The weeks before it decide.

wrong.Parabolic; the red close is the crack: The crack only matters on a parabolic run. This run was linear.
wrong.Not parabolic; it is above its 200-day: Our rule lets a parabolic short sit above the 200-day. The 200-day is not what rules this out; the shrinking weekly range is.
wrong.Parabolic; three weeks of range: Three weeks of range is not three weeks of expanding range. The middle week shrank.

questions.story: A strong leader at highs. The last three weekly ranges were 12.33, 5.27 and 13.33 points. Today it gaps up and closes red.
questions.simple: The read is not parabolic. The middle week's range shrank to 5.27, so the weekly ranges did not each grow.

deeper.trap: A single big red day at highs looks like a climax. The weeks before it decide. Two big weeks around one small week is a bumpy climb, not an accelerating one. Bracco warns that judging by percent gain alone, without structure, is a frequent mistake.

reasons: rests on the card's weekly-range form
figures come from our own scan

questions.q: A 4-day burst ends in a gap on day 5 and the day reverses. The burst ran down. Which trade is it?
choices: The Parabolic Long, on the turn up
The Parabolic Short, on the crack
No trade; no longs below the 200-day
A Wedge Drop, on the gap down
questions.answer: The Parabolic Long, on the turn up
questions.why: The Parabolic Long. It is the mirror image: a burst down, a gap down on the climax day, bought on the intraday turn. The stop sits under the low and the 9 EMA is above. Our rulebook calls the long the mirror of the short.
questions.lesson_line: Look which way the burst went. Down means the long, with everything flipped.

wrong.The Parabolic Short, on the crack: A short needs a burst up and a gap up. This burst ran down.
wrong.A Wedge Drop, on the gap down: A Wedge Drop comes after a 3 to 10 day stall at the 10-day EMA, and only below the 200-day. This is a burst down, not a stall.
wrong.No trade; no longs below the 200-day: Our 200-day rule has an exception for the parabolic long, the mirror image: a burst down.

questions.simple: A burst down into a gap down that reverses is the Parabolic Long, the mirror of the short, bought on the turn.

reasons: rests on the owner's mirror rule (B26)

questions.q: Which setup is that?
choices: A Wedge Drop on the breakdown
A Parabolic Short on the breakdown
A Parabolic Long on the breakdown
A News Failure on the breakdown
questions.answer: A Wedge Drop on the breakdown
questions.why: A Wedge Drop. It comes days later, after a 3 to 10 day stall within 1 ATR of the 10-day EMA. It is taken only below the 200-day. A Parabolic Short is taken on the climax day itself, far above its 200-day. The Wedge Drop sits on the averages.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the distance from the averages. The climax is far from them; the Wedge Drop sits on them.

wrong.A Parabolic Short on the breakdown: The climax day is far above the averages. This stock is sitting on them, days after its top.
wrong.A Parabolic Long on the breakdown: A long needs a burst down and a gap down. This is a stall after a top.
wrong.A News Failure on the breakdown: A News Failure is a good-news gap up that closes red. There was no gap here, just a stall and a break.

questions.story: A stock under its 200-day topped days ago, then stalled five days at its 10-day EMA. Today it broke down out of that stall.
questions.simple: This is a Wedge Drop. It comes days after the top, from a stall at the 10-day EMA under the 200-day.

deeper.trap: Both are shorts, so the names are easy to mix up. Ask two things: how far is the price from its averages, and is it above or below the 200-day? Far above on the climax day is the Parabolic Short. On the averages, days later, under the 200-day, is the Wedge Drop.

reasons: rests on the card's setup definitions

questions.q: Short 521.70, stop 565.54, the 9 EMA at 455.00. How many R is the cover at the 9 EMA?
questions.why: 1.52R. R is the stop minus the fill: 565.54 minus 521.70. The reward is the fill minus the target: 521.70 minus 455.00. Divide the reward by R to count the cover in R. The fill and stop are CGC's from our data. The 455.00 average is made up for the drill.
questions.lesson_line: Count the 9 EMA target in R before you short.
questions.simple: The cover is 1.52R, found by dividing the distance to the target by the distance to the stop.

reasons: a computed key (R multiple)
how much comes off at the 9 EMA is held (D-013); only the arithmetic is keyed

wrong.2.52R: Measured the reward from the stop instead of from the fill.
wrong.11.90R: Divided the fill price by R, the stop distance.
wrong.15.20R: Slipped the decimal point one place right.

questions.q: A stop over the climax high that is past 5% usually means waiting for a tighter trigger. You never pull the stop in to fit a size.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We prefer a stop 1-3% away, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% is acceptable. The climax high is often further: on our daily-bar examples GDS was 8.4%, BILI 7.2% and TPL 8.9% away. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. We never pull the stop in to fit a size.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop under the day's high.
questions.simple: True. The climax high is often far from the fill, so past 5 percent we wait for a tighter trigger and never squeeze the stop.

reasons: stop width options are held (D-005)
rests on the owner's size-from-the-stop rule (A5, A3)
the wider-than-3% claim comes from our own examples

questions.q: Our rule?
choices: No adding; one entry, one stop
Add half; improve average
Add if volume dries up
No adding; widen the stop
questions.answer: No adding; one entry, one stop
questions.why: No adding. The full size at one price with one stop. Bracco: parabolic advances often go further than anyone thinks, so he never adds when he is down. The stop is the exit and never moves wider, so widening it is no escape either.
questions.lesson_line: Averaging up a short is how a 1R loss becomes a blow-up.

wrong.Add half; improve average: A better average with a bigger position is a bigger squeeze.
wrong.Add if volume dries up: No condition opens the door. One entry, one stop, and the stop decides.
wrong.No adding; widen the stop: The stop is the exit. It only moves in your favor, never wider.

questions.story: Your short is nearly 1R against you, still under the day's high. A friend says average up, the top is in.
questions.simple: No adding. We take one entry at full size with one stop, because parabolic runs often go further than anyone thinks.

reasons: rests on the owner's one-entry and stop rules (A5, A4)

questions.q: By Bracco, when do these climax moves often peak or unwind?
choices: Thursday or Friday, monthly expiry
The very first day of a new rally
A quiet week with no hype at all
The first week out of a long base
questions.answer: Thursday or Friday, monthly expiry
questions.why: Thursdays or Fridays, especially right before or on monthly option expirations. That is Bracco's observation. Our card lists it as a cue, along with a short-term stretched index. These are cues, not triggers.
questions.lesson_line: Bracco watches Thursdays and Fridays into monthly expiration. It is a cue, not a trigger.

wrong.The very first day of a new rally: Climaxes end cycles: Bracco says a cycle ends with the leaders going parabolic. A rally's first day has stretched nothing.
wrong.A quiet week with no hype at all: No hype, no crowd to exhaust. Bracco ties these tops to a cycle ending with leaders going parabolic.
wrong.The first week out of a long base: Week one out of a base is too early. Our card says that is not this setup.

questions.simple: Bracco says these moves often peak or unwind on Thursdays or Fridays, especially right before or on monthly option expirations.

deeper.trap: Expiration week is a cue, not a trigger. A Thursday or Friday into expiration with no gap up, no crack and no burst is still not a trade. The cue only adds context to a climax that already meets the rules.

reasons: the context cues are the card's proposal (D-023 pending)
an options-calendar cue

questions.q: What was the mistake?
choices: Shorted strength: no crack, no burst
None; any gap up is a climax
The stop over the high was tight
Entered late; open was the entry
questions.answer: Shorted strength: no crack, no burst
questions.why: Shorting strength. The day closed above its open, so there was no crack, and one box is no burst. On daily bars a close under the open is the stand-in for the crack. Shorting a green climax day won 23% of the time. Shorting that close lost 4.5R on the next day's gap up.
questions.lesson_line: A green close with one box is strength. Shorting strength pays in R, the wrong way.

wrong.None; any gap up is a climax: A gap up that closes green has not cracked. The gap is the setup, the crack is the trigger.
wrong.The stop over the high was tight: Nothing in the story says the stop was wrong. The mistake was the entry: a green day with one box.
wrong.Entered late; open was the entry: Nothing at the open on the climax day. The mistake was what you shorted: a green close with one box.

questions.story: The stock gaps up 2.2% and closes 7.3% above its open. Only one burst box is checked. You short the close anyway.
questions.simple: The mistake was shorting strength. The day closed above its open, so there was no crack, and one box is no burst.

reasons: figures come from our own scan

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Bracco: most climax points come at obvious ___ numbers.
questions.answer: round
questions.why: Round. Bracco: most of these climax points occur around very obvious, round numbers. Our card adds that a chart parabolic even on a log scale is the strong form. It is a cue, not a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Watch the big round numbers. Bracco sees many climaxes there.
questions.simple: Bracco says most climax points come at very obvious round numbers.

reasons: the log-scale form is the card's cue

questions.q: Where was the error?
choices: Calling a top on a young run
Placing the stop over the high
Not holding past the new high
Using the 9 EMA as the target
questions.answer: Calling a top on a young run
questions.why: Calling a top on a young run: shorting a stock fresh out of a base. Bracco: a very short lived trade if it set up. RGTI had only 2 up closes before a 3.9% gap, reached the 9 EMA on day 5 at 0.99R, then a new high on day 6 took the stop. The stop and the target did their jobs. The context was wrong.
questions.lesson_line: Right candle, wrong week. A stock just out of a base has fuel.

wrong.Not holding past the new high: Over the high you are wrong. Holding through it is the blow-up.
wrong.Placing the stop over the high: A few cents over the high is the rule. It did its job on day 6.
wrong.Using the 9 EMA as the target: The target was right and it was reached. The context was wrong.

questions.story: Fresh out of a base: two up days, then a 3.9% gap that closes red. You short 31.64, stop 34.44. Day 5 touches the 9 EMA at 0.99R; day 6 a new high takes the stop.
questions.simple: The error was shorting a stock fresh out of a base. It had fuel left, and a new high on day 6 hit the stop.

deeper.trap: The 9 EMA was reached at 0.99R, so the trade looks almost fine, and only 1.14R was ever available. That is the trap: a near-miss on the numbers hides a wrong setup. Right candle, wrong week.

reasons: figures come from our own scan

questions.q: Where should the short have been?
choices: At the VWAP break, after the turn
At the close; it is five stars
At the break of the day's low
Nowhere; five-star climaxes are traps
questions.answer: At the VWAP break, after the turn
questions.why: At the VWAP break, after the turn. On this climax, SMCI on 2024-02-16, a short at the close put the stop 34.3% away and ran only 0.40R at best. A new high on day 10 took it. The VWAP break at 90.01 ran 1.16R before the same stop at 107.90. Even so, that stop is past the 5% we accept, so we would mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: The entry is the VWAP break after the turn. Not the close of the climax day.

wrong.At the close; it is five stars: Five stars does not fix a 34.3% stop. Past 5%, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
wrong.Nowhere; five-star climaxes are traps: Five stars grades the setup, and its four boxes were real. The entry at the close was the problem; the VWAP break ran 1.16R against 0.40R.
wrong.At the break of the day's low: That is Bracco's second entry, which we do not take. We use one entry, at the VWAP break.

questions.story: Bracco's five-star climax, four of four boxes. The day closed at the low. A short at the close, 80.33, puts the stop at 107.90, 34.3% away.
questions.simple: Short at the VWAP break after the turn, since a short at the close puts the stop 34.3 percent away.

deeper.counter: Five stars grades the setup, not the entry. SMCI's four of four boxes were real, and it was Bracco's own five-star example, yet the close-entry short lost. Grade and entry are two separate decisions.

reasons: numbers come from one dossier row read off our own bars (the examples are unreviewed)
stop width options are held (D-005)
fixed before

questions.q: Kullamagi wants a smaller cap up 300% to 1,000% or more before he calls it a parabolic short candidate.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A stock up 50-100%+ in days or weeks if larger cap, or 300-1000%+ if smaller cap. Small caps need a far bigger run.
questions.lesson_line: The smaller the stock, the bigger the run it takes to exhaust.

questions.q: What rule capped the damage?
choices: The window and three tries a week
No rule; three losses is a mistake
The 2R gap ceiling
questions.answer: The window and three tries a week
questions.why: The 1 to 2 day window and the cap of 3 tries in a week. Bracco: 3 failed attempts over 2 sessions, no revenge trade, no averaging down. Then he dropped it.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries, no revenge, no adding. Then walk away.

wrong.No rule; three losses is a mistake: Three planned losses inside the window is the rule working. Revenge-shorting would be the mistake.
wrong.The 2R gap ceiling: No gap through the stop here. Each stop was taken in the session.

questions.story: Bracco shorted AGQ three times in two sessions and was stopped each time. He did not add and did not revenge trade.

questions.q: Is the short allowed under our 200-day rule?
choices: Yes; shorts there need no exception
Yes; but only if the 200-day points down
No; a parabolic short must be above it
No; a gap up is a sign of strength
questions.answer: Yes; shorts there need no exception
questions.why: Yes. Our rule is shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless the short is a parabolic short. This stock is below its 200-day, so the short needs no exception. The exception matters only above the line, where our card puts a climax. Being below the line is not enough alone. The short still needs its own trigger and stop.
questions.lesson_line: Below the 200-day a short needs no excuse. Above it, only the parabolic one.

wrong.No; a parabolic short must be above it: The exception lets a parabolic short sit above the line. It does not bar a short below it.
wrong.Yes; but only if the 200-day points down: The rule asks where the stock sits, not which way the line points.
wrong.No; a gap up is a sign of strength: The 200-day rule looks at where the stock sits, not at the gap. Below the line a short is allowed. The gap is part of the setup.

questions.story: A stock below its 200-day rips higher in a burst, then ends with a 6% gap up and a closing reversal.
questions.simple: Yes, because a short below the 200-day needs no exception, and this stock is below it.

deeper.trap: Below the 200-day does not mean parabolic. The line only decides whether a short is allowed at all. The burst, the gap and the VWAP trigger still have to be there.

reasons: one cited fact only (B26, h01) carries the key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
the exception test above the line is held (D-040)
fixed before (the CAR example was removed)

questions.q: Short 48.50, stop 52.56. The stock gaps over the stop and the first 30-minute high is 53.40. How many R is the loss there?
questions.why: 1.21R. The 30-minute high minus the fill, over the stop minus the fill. Inside the 2R ceiling, so 53.40 is the new stop, not an exit.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap in R. Under 2R the 30-minute high is the stop; past it, you are out.

questions.q: Bracco: the climax day almost always shows the highest OPENING volume of the whole run.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Opening volume rises over several days, with the climax day almost invariably showing the highest opening volume of the entire run. Range and volume expansion come first.
questions.lesson_line: The biggest open of the run is the crowd arriving. That is who you sell to.

questions.q: By our card, is it the climax-day short?
choices: No; it never gapped up that day
Yes; the red close is the crack
Yes; record volume is enough
No; a burst needs five up days
questions.answer: No; it never gapped up that day
questions.why: No. The climax day must open above the prior close, and Bracco will not short without that gap up. Our card says no gap up means it is not this setup. A red close on record volume without the gap is not this trade.
questions.lesson_line: The gap is the exhaustion. Without it the day is just a red day.

wrong.Yes; the red close is the crack: The crack only counts after the gap. The gap is a required box.
wrong.Yes; record volume is enough: Volume adds strength to a climax that gapped up. The gap is the gate.
wrong.No; a burst needs five up days: A burst is a 3 to 5 day move, so four days fits. The missing gap is the problem.

questions.story: A four-day burst. Day five opens under the prior close, runs up, then closes red on record volume.
questions.simple: No. The climax day has to open above the prior close, and a red close on record volume does not replace the gap.

deeper.trap: A red close on record volume feels like a climax. Do not let it talk you in. The gap up is the exhaustion, and without it the day is just a red day. Bracco: he will not short without that gap-up.

reasons: the gap is a required box by Bracco and the card, which other sources do not require
rests on the owner's burst definition (B26)

questions.q: What does the card teach from it?
choices: The time limit; the gap was small
Hold five weeks; it hit 2.95R
A 2.8% gap is a strong A+ cue
A low close means it falls
questions.answer: The time limit; the gap was small
questions.why: The time limit, and a small gap grades lower. This climax had four boxes and a close at the day's low, but only a 2.8% gap. That is a weak mark on our card, where 5% or more is the A+ row. The card says to cover if the 9 EMA is not reached within 3 sessions of entry. Here the 9 EMA took 8 sessions, and the stock chopped under the climax high for five weeks. It reached 2.95R at best, but not by the plan.
questions.lesson_line: No 9 EMA within three sessions means the climax is out of time. Cover and move on.

wrong.Hold five weeks; it hit 2.95R: It reached 2.95R at best, but the 9 EMA took 8 sessions. The card's limit is 3.
wrong.A 2.8% gap is a strong A+ cue: A gap of 5% or more is the A+ cue. A small gap is the weak point.
wrong.A low close means it falls: A close at the low is not a promise. This one closed at the low and still chopped under its high for five weeks.

questions.story: Four of four boxes and a close at the day's low, but the gap was 2.8%. Short 502.85, stop 547.76. The stock chops under its high for five weeks.
questions.simple: The card teaches the time limit, because the cover is due in 3 sessions and this one chopped for five weeks.

deeper.trap: Do not take 2.95R as proof that holding works. It was the best point, and the trade took 8 sessions to reach the 9 EMA, with five weeks of chop under the high. One slow winner does not cancel a 3-session limit.

reasons: the 3-session cover is the dossier's proposed rule (ps.time_limit), not yet the owner's
numbers come from one dossier row read off our own bars (the examples are unreviewed)
fixed before

questions.q: Bracco's name for that, and his view of it?
choices: Quick range breakdown; not a fan
The U-Turn, which he likes best
A five-star climax; best of all
Long-drawn-out range; he avoids it
questions.answer: Quick range breakdown; not a fan
questions.why: The Quick Opening Range Breakdown: the high is set on the first 5-minute candle, then the 2- or 5-minute opening range breaks. Bracco says he is not particularly fond of it. It is less frequent and more challenging. It often appears on day 1 or 2 of the burst, typically too early in the move.
questions.lesson_line: A top on the first candle of day two is usually not the top.

wrong.The U-Turn, which he likes best: The U-Turn runs higher first and turns 10 to 60 minutes in. This topped on the first candle.
wrong.A five-star climax; best of all: Day two of a burst is early. The climax gap usually comes on day 3 to 5.
wrong.Long-drawn-out range; he avoids it: That one is a tight range for the first one to two hours. This topped on the first candle, so the name is wrong.

questions.story: Day two of a burst: two up days. Today it gaps up, sets its high on the first 5-minute candle and breaks the opening range low.
questions.simple: It is the Quick Opening Range Breakdown, which Bracco is not fond of and which often comes too early.

deeper.trap: Count the days before you trust a first-candle top. The climax gap usually comes on day 3 to 5 of the burst. On day 1 or 2 the same shape is typically too early in the move.

reasons: one author's view (Bracco), cited from the post's own words
fixed before: the key said weakest and least liked, which the post does not say; it now says not fond

questions.q: Bracco: a frequent mistake is judging a stock by its percent gain alone and ignoring the chart's structure.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Relying solely on a stock's percentage gain, overlooking its chart structure and formation, is the mistake he names. A linear run, however far it has gone, is not this setup.
questions.lesson_line: The number gets you looking. The shape gets you the trade.

questions.q: What now?
choices: Out at once; past the 2R ceiling
New stop 74.00, the 30-minute high
Hold; it must come back to the 9 EMA
New stop 72.00, the opening price
questions.answer: Out at once; past the 2R ceiling
questions.why: Out. The first 30 minutes decide, with a ceiling: if they take the loss past 2R, get out. The open at 72.00 is far past that ceiling, against a 60.00 entry and a 63.00 stop. The 30-minute high of 74.00 is worse. The 30-minute high is the new stop only inside the ceiling. This is the failure mode: a squeeze gaps up over the stop for 4R to 5R losses.
questions.lesson_line: The gap rule has a ceiling. Past 2R there is nothing to wait for.

wrong.New stop 74.00, the 30-minute high: The 30-minute high is the new stop only inside 2R. This gap is far past 2R at the open.
wrong.Hold; it must come back to the 9 EMA: Nothing must. A squeeze gapping over the stop is how this setup takes 4R to 5R losses.
wrong.New stop 72.00, the opening price: The rule never uses the open as the stop. The 30-minute high is the new stop, and only inside 2R.

questions.story: You shorted the crack at 60.00, stop 63.00. Overnight news; it opens at 72.00 and the first 30-minute high is 74.00.
questions.simple: Get out. The gap already took the loss past 2R, and the rule says past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you leave.

deeper.trap: Nothing guarantees the stock returns to the 9 EMA. The gap rule is not a way to wait. It is a short window with a hard ceiling. Past 2R the plan is over, and a gap over the stop is the one way this setup does real damage.

reasons: rests on the owner's gap rule and its 2R ceiling (B20)
the key needs a loss worked out from the story

questions.q: Four boxes and record volume, but the climax gap is only 1.7%, like SCHW in 1999. Does the small gap rule it out?
choices: Not ruled out; a small gap grades lower
Ruled out; a gap must be 5% or more
Ruled out; small gaps lack exhaustion
Not ruled out; size is never graded
questions.answer: Not ruled out; a small gap grades lower
questions.why: Not ruled out. Our card requires the climax day to open above the prior close, and 1.7% does. A gap of 5% or more is the stronger A+ row, so 1.7% is a weaker mark, not a fail. SCHW in 1999 had four boxes and three record-volume days. It reached the 9 EMA the next session, and the 1.7% gap was its weak point.
questions.lesson_line: Any open above the prior close is enough. A big gap grades higher.

wrong.Ruled out; a gap must be 5% or more: 5% is the stronger mark, not the requirement. The requirement is any open above the prior close.
wrong.Ruled out; small gaps lack exhaustion: SCHW's 1.7% gap came with four boxes, three record-volume days and the 9 EMA the next session. A small gap lowers one mark. It does not cancel the rest.
wrong.Not ruled out; size is never graded: Size is graded. A gap of 5% or more is the A+ row; a small one is a B- mark.

questions.simple: Not ruled out, because any open above the prior close meets the rule, and a gap of 5 percent or more only grades higher.

deeper.trap: Do not read weak as skip. SCHW's 1.7% gap was the weak point. Yet it had four boxes and three record-volume days, and it reached the 9 EMA the next session. One weak mark lowers the grade. It does not cancel the others.

reasons: rests on the criteria card's grade rows (grading is discretionary, E50)
fixed before
the count of boxes needed is held (D-040)

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, target.
choices: Market now; stop over the high; 9 EMA
Short the open; stop 3%; cover at 3R
Wait for the close; stop at the 9 EMA
Market now; stop at the VWAP; 9 EMA
questions.answer: Market now; stop over the high; 9 EMA
questions.why: Market now, stop a few cents over the day's high, target the daily 9 EMA. Our entries are market orders. The trigger is the break back under VWAP after the high is set. The stop sits a few cents over the climax day's high at entry. GDS: the daily stand-in short was 48.50 with the stop at 52.56, and the 9 EMA came in 2 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Entry at the VWAP break, stop over the high, out at the 9 EMA.

wrong.Short the open; stop 3%; cover at 3R: Nothing at the open, the stop is a level not a percent, and the target is the 9 EMA.
wrong.Wait for the close; stop at the 9 EMA: The close is a daily stand-in, not the trade. And the 9 EMA is below the price; it is the target.
wrong.Market now; stop at the VWAP; 9 EMA: A VWAP reclaim is Kullamagi's exit for a VWAP-fail entry. For the VWAP-break entry the stop sits a few cents over the day's high.

questions.story: GDS, February 2025: a 13-session run from a flat base, four of four boxes, a 15% gap on record volume. On the 5-minute chart it runs, then breaks VWAP.
questions.simple: Enter at market on the VWAP break, put the stop just over the day's high, and aim for the daily 9 EMA.

deeper.example: GDS gapped up 15.4% on 2025-02-20 on record volume and closed red. Our daily stand-in for the plan was a short at 48.50 with the stop at 52.56. On the 5-minute chart the same plan starts earlier, at the VWAP break.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 and D47)

questions.q: Hidden ticker, after a burst. The last bar is the climax day. Read the bar: take it or pass?
choices: Take it; a gap up that closed red
Take it; short the next day's open
Pass; the day closed green, not red
Pass; there was no gap up today
questions.answer: Take it; a gap up that closed red
questions.why: Take it. The last bar opened above the prior close and closed red, in the lower half of its range. It came after a 13-session run with four of four boxes.
